clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant primary lymphoedema caused by variants in FLT4, which encodes the lymphatic growth factor receptor VEGFR3
It presents as congenital, usually bilateral, lower-limb lymphoedema, characteristically confined below the knee and often affecting the dorsum of the feet
Suggestive signs include upturned toenails, deep skin creases at the toes, prominent leg veins and, in males, hydrocele
Onset at or shortly after birth distinguishes it from FOXC2-related lymphoedema-distichiasis, which typically begins around puberty
The underlying defect is hypoplasia and functional failure of the initial lymphatics due to impaired VEGFR3 signalling
Recurrent cellulitis is a common and important complication of the affected limbs
Diagnosis rests on the congenital clinical picture, family history and FLT4 genetic testing, with lymphoscintigraphy showing impaired uptake
Management is lifelong supportive lymphoedema care with compression, meticulous skin care and prompt treatment of infection
reference.pathophysiology: Milroy disease is an autosomal dominant primary lymphoedema arising from loss-of-function variants in FLT4 (VEGFR3), the receptor for vascular endothelial growth factors C and D that drives development of the lymphatic vasculature. Defective VEGFR3 signalling causes hypoplasia and functional failure of the initial (peripheral) lymphatic vessels, so interstitial fluid cannot be adequately drained from the lower limbs, producing congenital, typically bilateral, below-knee lymphoedema. The chronic protein-rich oedema predisposes to skin changes and recurrent infection.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital venous malformation with limb swelling
additionalInvestigations: Lymphoscintigraphy demonstrating reduced or absent lymphatic uptake
Clinical examination for toenail changes, toe creases and hydrocele
Duplex ultrasound to exclude a venous cause of swelling
Assessment for and monitoring of recurrent cellulitis
Family history review and cascade genetic screening
redFlags: Recurrent or severe cellulitis of the affected limb
Rapidly progressive or asymmetric swelling suggesting an additional secondary cause
Signs of chronic infection or systemic sepsis
New unilateral swelling in a previously stable patient warranting further evaluation
reference.prognosis: Milroy disease is a chronic lifelong condition but is compatible with normal life expectancy; with consistent conservative lymphoedema management most patients maintain good limb function, though recurrent cellulitis and progressive skin changes are the main sources of morbidity.
pitfalls: Confusing it with the later-onset FOXC2 lymphoedema-distichiasis syndrome
Overlooking supportive clues such as upturned toenails and hydrocele
Delaying treatment of cellulitis, which accelerates lymphatic damage
Failing to provide genetic counselling for an autosomal dominant disorder
references: Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies: Haemangiomas and Malformations
management: Manage the lymphoedema conservatively with graduated compression garments, bandaging and complex decongestive therapy including manual lymphatic drainage and exercise
Maintain meticulous skin care and limb elevation to limit progression and protect the skin
Treat episodes of cellulitis promptly with antibiotics and offer prophylactic antibiotics for recurrent attacks
Consider microsurgical options such as lymphovenous anastomosis in carefully selected patients
Manage associated features such as hydrocele surgically where symptomatic
Provide genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant FLT4/VEGFR3 disorder and offer cascade family screening
Follow up long-term through a specialist lymphoedema service
